These are the divine chastisements that exposed the work of sin in the heart, indeed in the whole man: spiritual hunger, dryness, attack by insects that spoil the fruit, infection with spiritual diseases, the shattering of gifts (the young men), deprivation of freedom (the taking away of the horses), the rising of the smell of corruption and stench, and destruction by the fires of deadly thunderbolts! But the purpose of these chastisements is: "Prepare to meet thy God, O Israel" [12].

12 "Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel." 13 For, lo, he that formeth the mountains, and createth the wind, and declareth unto man what is his thought, that maketh the morning darkness, and treadeth upon the high places of the earth, The LORD, The God of hosts, is his name.

God's chastisements exposed our corrupt state, as though by the surgeon's scalpel that opened the wound to reveal the stench hidden in the body. And now how is the wound to be bandaged, and our state mended? Or, as He said: how is "prepare to meet thy God, O Israel" to be fulfilled? He answers: "For, lo, he that formeth the mountains, and createth the wind (the Spirit), and declareth unto man what is his thought (his Christ), that maketh the morning darkness, and treadeth upon the high places of the earth, The LORD, The God of hosts, is his name" [13].

The Lord of glory says: "Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?" (Lk 14:31). If Israel has entered into a dispute against God, let it know who God is and what His capabilities are, or else let it make peace with Him! Here the prophet declares that God is the maker of the mountains. If kings take refuge in firm mountains during war, God does not take refuge in them but is their Creator. As the psalmist says: "O LORD God of hosts, who is a strong LORD like unto thee? or to thy faithfulness round about thee? Thou rulest the raging of the sea: when the waves thereof arise, thou stillest them... The heavens are thine, the earth also is thine: as for the world and the fulness thereof, thou hast founded them" (Ps 89:8-11). If armies find their salvation in the mountains, God is the founder of the whole world.
He says: "createth the wind," and in the Septuagint "createth the spirit." The Creator of the wind, about which the army commander is concerned before the beginning of the battle, is God Himself.

He makes the dawn (the morning) darkness, because He sends His thick cloud, which covers the earth and hides the light, and He is the One who walks on the high places of the earth, or its lofty peaks... He is Yahweh, who cannot be comprehended or expressed! This is your God, whom you must prepare to meet, O Israel, not for dispute but for reconciliation!

The text came in the Septuagint thus: "He who establishes the thunder and creates the spirit and declares to man his Christ." Many of the Fathers, such as St. Augustine, see that this text carries a clear prophecy about the Messianic age, for the new Israel prepares to meet its God through the Father's declaring of His Christ to man, so that man receives Him as the mystery of reconciliation between the Father and man.

Some heretics tried to use this text to claim that the Holy Spirit is a creature, since it says "creates the spirit." Many of the Fathers answered them, among them St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, who says: [It is fitting for us to understand that the prophet speaks of the creation of another spirit in His establishing of the thunder, and not of the creation of the Holy Spirit. For the name "thunder" has been given in the mystical language of the Gospel. Those in whom faith in the Gospel is established without shaking pass from the flesh to the spirit, as the Lord says: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit" (Jn 3:6). It is God who establishes the voice of the Gospel and makes man spirit (spiritual); whoever is born of the Spirit and becomes spirit, to him Christ is declared, as the Apostle says: "No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost" (1 Cor 12:3).]

This is the secret of the new Israel's meeting: God establishes the thunder, that is, He sends us the word of preaching that thunders in the soul, and creates in us the spiritual nature instead of the fleshly life, so that Christ, the Lord of glory, is declared in us by His Holy Spirit!

By this the prophet turned the mind of Israel from the harsh chastisements, which could not bring them back to God but only exposed their weakness and the work of sin in them, to the Messiah the Savior, whom the Father declares to man, so that he receives Him by the Holy Spirit as Redeemer and Savior!

The third sermon begins with a lamentation over the virgin of Israel: 1 Hear ye this word which I take up against you, even a lamentation, O house of Israel. 2 "The virgin of Israel is fallen; she shall no more rise:
she is forsaken upon her land; there is none to raise her up." 3 For thus saith the Lord GOD;
"The city that went out by a thousand shall leave an hundred, and that which went forth by an hundred shall leave ten, to the house of Israel." [1-3].

The word before us is a lamentation which the Lord Himself raised, describing with sorrow the state to which the virgin of Israel had come. Perhaps He called Israel a "virgin" to declare that this lamentation, which is raised over one who has died, was raised over the virgin of Israel, who is like a bride who died in her early youth while still a virgin, before she could enjoy the joy of married life. She is the virgin from whom the Lord expected to have a perpetual bride, but she chose the path of spiritual death, and so lost her life before she could enjoy the life of union with her Bridegroom.

Perhaps God called her "the virgin of Israel" as a sign that until this moment she had been the virgin who had not yet been defeated and had not yet fallen under captivity... But by her evil she loses her virginity, indeed she loses all her life. God has a jealousy for her because she is His virgin bride, and the Apostle Paul bore the spirit of his Master when he said: "For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ" (2 Cor 11:1-2).

The virgin of Israel fell from what she ought to have been, a virgin for the Lord who bears His holiness and His splendor. Sadly she fell and shall no more rise, because she refuses the chastisements of her Bridegroom meant to bring her back to Him; she relied on herself or on others apart from her Bridegroom, and so found no one to raise her up. She was cast down upon her land, a sign of complete weakness, for she did not go out to fight, nor did she withdraw to an outside battlefield, but was defeated before herself, because of her inner weakness. As the Lord Himself says: "A man's foes shall be they of his own household" (Mt 10:36). In our inner Jerusalem we fall when we accept the ego and live for ourselves, not for the Lord who loves us!

When a person falls in his inner battle because of the ego, which seeks its own and not what belongs to others, he loses much; if it goes out by a thousand there remain a hundred, and if it goes out by a hundred there remain ten... It loses much, and the small faithful remnant remains preserved with God. This remnant, which represents the tenth in God's eyes, is dear and precious, and He is bound to preserve it for the sake of His faithfulness toward His believers, as we have seen more clearly in more than one place in our study of the book of Ezekiel.

God does not forget the hundred for the sake of the remnant of the thousand, nor the ten for the sake of the remnant of the hundred. He did not forget Lot and his two daughters for the sake of the whole region of Sodom and Gomorrah, nor did He forget Noah and his family for the sake of the corruption of the whole world!

entries.section: 2. Seek the Lord, not the idol:

paragraphs.text: 4 For thus saith the LORD unto the house of Israel, "Seek ye me, and ye shall live: 5 But seek not Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and pass not to Beersheba: for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nought. 6 Seek the LORD, and ye shall live; lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and devour it, and there be none to quench it in Bethel. 7 Ye who turn judgment to wormwood, and leave off righteousness in the earth, 8 Seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning, and maketh the day dark with night: that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The LORD is his name: 9 That strengtheneth the spoiled against the strong, so that the spoiled shall come against the fortress."

Having raised a lamentation over the virgin of Israel, He did not stop at the sorrowful description, but revealed the door of deliverance, by turning to God, the Source of life, and abandoning idolatrous worship, saying: "Seek ye me, and ye shall live: but seek not Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and pass not to Beersheba" [4-5].

At that time the people bore the outward marks of religiosity, going out to worship at the holy places, but it appears that the worship of God had become mixed with idolatrous worship, especially in the principal centers of Israel: Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba. Or perhaps their worship had become merely a soothing of consciences: they went to those places and offered much to God, but they did not seek Him with their heart, nor keep His commandment in their life and conduct. As I have said before, ritual was separated from the spiritual life among them, and their worship became a means of covering up their wicked attitudes.

If we seek the holy places, let our first and last seeking in them be life with God and in Him: "Seek ye me, and ye shall live." Note that the word "seek" does not mean merely asking with the mouth, but the true inner longing for God, the secret of our true life.

As St. Augustine says, addressing God, the secret of his life: [How then shall I seek You, O Lord? For when I seek You, my God, I seek the happy life. I seek You that my soul may live, for my body lives by my soul, and my soul lives by You.]

Places that were once holy became a stumbling block through idolatrous worship, so He says: "For Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nought." Gilgal and Bethel were two holy places, but since man corrupted them, the first place is taken captive and the second is utterly destroyed. When the Samaritan woman said to the Lord Jesus: "Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship" (Jn 4:20), the Master answered her: "Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father... God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth" (Jn 4:21, 24).

We do not deny that God is pleased even with the holy places which man offers in love to be places of worship for Him, but He rejoices in them for the sake of the person who is sanctified by Him! Even in the consecrated church the heart of the believer rises above all limits of place and time to soar toward eternity, and finds the Spirit of God has lifted him up into heaven itself! I have spoken often before about the church building, its meaning, and its connection with the inner life of the soul as well as with the heavenly and liturgical life. If the house of God loses its spiritual meaning and man is confined to dust and earth, he turns the house of God into an obstacle instead of being the secret of the soul's soaring!

entries.section: 2. Seek the Lord, not the idol:

paragraphs.text: The Lord repeats, "Seek the LORD, and ye shall live" [6]. This is the goal of all our worship: to meet our Lord Jesus and seek Him with all the heart as the secret of our life.

The Lord threatens: "Lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and devour it, and there be none to quench it in Bethel" [6]. Perhaps many of the tribes of Israel used to count the sons of Joseph blessed because the mountain of Bethel had fallen to their lot (Josh 16:1-2), but this mountain became a consuming fire when it was misused. Perhaps it is like the priesthood, which gives a person mighty spiritual and pastoral possibilities, but if it is misused it becomes the very weapon of destruction. And why speak of Bethel or the priesthood, when the Lord Christ Himself, who is the secret of the salvation of many, became by His coming a cause of judgment for those who denied Him, as He says: "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloak for their sin... If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin: but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father" (Jn 15:22-24). As the Apostle Paul says of the Lord Christ: "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish: to the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life" (2 Cor 2:15-16).

entries.section: 2. Seek the Lord, not the idol:

paragraphs.text: We return to Israel and find that it had mixed the worship of the living God with idolatrous worship, so that Bethel became destruction for the house of Joseph, and here by this is meant all Israel coming to Bethel, for their lives are set ablaze with the fire of evil and there is no one able to quench it. Thus they turn truth into the bitterness of injustice and corrupt heavenly righteousness by casting it to the ground: "Ye who turn judgment to wormwood, and leave off righteousness in the earth" [7].

If wormwood is an exceedingly bitter herb thrown on the ground, which man cannot bear, then the truth, which gladdens the heart of God and man, when it is overturned is turned into its opposite and becomes wormwood. So it is with those who have great abilities and gifts: when they are sanctified by the Spirit of truth, mingled with love and humility, they bear witness to the truth and offer, by the Holy Spirit, works to which generations testify and which heaven confirms; but when they go astray they do not stand passive, rather they become bitter wormwood in the mouth of God and His Church, turned into instruments of demolition instead of building. They cast righteousness to the ground, since their thinking burdens them, without their knowing it, with a deadly earthly nature.
Therefore let "the LORD" Himself be the object of our constant seeking that we may live, and let us not turn into wormwood or cast righteousness into the dust... But who is this Lord whom we seek?
"He that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning, and maketh the day dark with night:
that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The LORD is his name:

entries.section: 2. Seek the Lord, not the idol:

paragraphs.text: That strengtheneth the spoiled against the strong, so that the spoiled shall come against the fortress" [8-9].

First: the Creator of the Pleiades and the Giant, which are two groups of stars that were famous at that time. If Israel had turned aside to worship the stars, then the true God is the Creator of all the stars, and it is He whom it is fitting for them to seek.

The Septuagint rendering of the text brings out that God is the Creator of things and also the One who changes them... St. John Chrysostom has a very bold word, for he sees in God the Creator One who trains us, His children, in the creative life, saying: [God gave us a body from the earth, but so that we might carry it with us to heaven. It is truly an earthly body, but it must be heavenly... It is as though He says: I created heaven and earth, and I gave you the authority to create. Make your earth heaven, for this is within your authority. I am the Creator of things and the One who upholds them [8]. As the Lord Himself says, He gave man a similar authority, as though He were an artist and a tender father teaching his son his art! I created your body beautiful and gave you authority to make something better... For if you cannot create a man, yet you are able (by the Holy Spirit) to make him righteous and acceptable before God. I formed the matter, so you adorn the will! Behold how I love you and entrust to you authority in great matters! Behold what honor is ours!]

Second: the God whom we seek turns the shadow of death (the night) into morning, and makes the day dark as night. He is not only the Creator of heaven and earth out of nothing, but He also brings about change: He changes night into morning, and day into night.

What is this night, or what He called the shadow of death which was turned into morning, but the fulfillment of the prophecies of the Old Testament and the shadows of the Law, when man had fallen under death as one in the night, into the day of His joyful coming, so that we were enlightened by His divine light? As the prophet says: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined" (Isa 9:2).

Let us offer Him our night and He will make it morning; let us hand over to Him all our troubles and sorrows, and He will shine upon us, and they will be turned into spiritual delights, surpassing peace, and glorious joy unspeakable.

As for the day which is made dark and becomes night, it reminds us of the divine work during the hours of the crucifixion, when noon turned into darkness because of our sins, which our Redeemer carried on His shoulders. This is the surpassing work of the Lord, who bore our sins in Himself, He who knew no sin!

And what is the day that becomes darkness but the day of the wicked, who live in the luxury and pleasures of life, reckoning that the joy of the world does not pass away and that their pleasures never end... But in His love He turns their day into night through His chastisements, which seem harsh, so that they may not be attached to the day of the world and its pleasures!

Third: He calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth... that is, He turns the waters of the seas into clouds that cover the earth and rain upon it. We saw in our study of the book of Joel [2:23] that the former rain and the latter rain refer to the grace of the Holy Spirit working in the children of God. So the God whom we seek is the Creator, and He is the One who changes our life by the coming of the Messiah the Savior, and He is the Giver of fruit through the waters of the Holy Spirit, as the Master Himself said: "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. (But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given)" (Jn 7:37-39).
Though we are earth, the waters of the Holy Spirit turn us into the delightful paradise of God, bearing the fruit of His Spirit in us!

Fourth: the God whom we seek, His name is Jehovah (Yahweh). After presenting Himself to us as Creator and Renewer of our nature through the saving work of Christ, and as the Giver of fruit in us by His Holy Spirit, He brought us into His mysteries... He is Yahweh, that is "the One who is," who cannot be comprehended. Though He has drawn very near to us through His saving work and the sending of His Holy Spirit, He remains the God who cannot be approached in the fullness of His essence. We spoke before about the meaning of the name of God "Yahweh" in our study of the book of Exodus (ch. 3).

entries.section: 2. Seek the Lord, not the idol:

paragraphs.text: Fifth: the God whom we seek is He "that strengtheneth the spoiled against the strong, so that the spoiled shall come against the fortress" [9]. He gives success and strength to the person who has been robbed or plundered against the strong man who wronged him, so that he is able to attack his fortress and recover his stolen right. He is the God who gives victory to the defeated soul and grants it strength and triumph!

entries.section: 3. Injustice in the courts of justice:

paragraphs.text: 10 They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly. 11 Forasmuch therefore as your treading is upon the poor, and ye take from him burdens of wheat: ye have built houses of hewn stone, but ye shall not dwell in them; ye have planted pleasant vineyards, but ye shall not drink wine of them. 12 For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right. 13 Therefore the prudent shall keep silence in that time; for it is an evil time. 14 Seek good, and not evil, that ye may live: and so the LORD, the God of hosts, shall be with you, as ye have spoken. 15 Hate the evil, and love the good, and establish judgment in the gate: it may be that the LORD God of hosts will be gracious unto the remnant of Joseph.

Among the Jews the courts of justice were held in a public square at the gate of the city (Deut 22:15; Isa 29:21), under the leadership of a judge or prophet who rebuked the wrongdoer and supported the righteous. But sadly the courts of justice were turned into courts of injustice. He says:

"They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly. Forasmuch therefore as your treading is upon the poor, and ye take from him burdens of wheat: ye have built houses of hewn stone, but ye shall not dwell in them; ye have planted pleasant vineyards, but ye shall not drink wine of them. For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right" [10-12].

These are painful manifestations of the injustice that prevailed in the courts of justice. On the one hand, instead of rebuking the wrongdoers, these elders hated the one who rebuked or warned them; they wanted to flatter the wrongdoers at the expense of the truth, so that they hated anyone who spoke a word of truth, because it wounds the rich wrongdoers. On the other hand, instead of lifting the needy from the dunghill, they trampled him underfoot. They demanded of him a gift that was closer to a bribe, and since he had no money to give, they compelled him to give his wheat, and he and his family remained hungry. The Law forbade usury on food (Deut 23:9). Yet these seize the food of the poor so that they may build for themselves houses of hewn stone that cannot give them security, and plant for themselves pleasant vineyards that cannot quench them with the wine of joy.
Finally, in their injustice they afflict the just and take the bribe which the Law forbids (Ex 21:30; Num 35:31).

entries.section: 3. Injustice in the courts of justice:

paragraphs.text: And since injustice increased greatly, even in the courts of justice, it was said: "Therefore the prudent shall keep silence in that time; for it is an evil time" [13]. When a person realizes that his defense of the needy is of no avail, he keeps silent, not out of cowardice or fear of the wrongdoers, but out of wisdom, so as not to waste his time on what is of no avail. St. Basil wrote at the end of his book "On the Holy Spirit," saying: [Since the ordinances of the Gospel have been utterly confused by disorder, the rush to advance to the chief offices has become beyond imagining, and every lover of display puts himself forward before others by force... So the entreaties of the leaders have become barren and vain, because everyone in the seas of his ignorance judges that it is his duty to give orders to others and not to obey anyone himself. For these reasons I have preferred silence to speech, for there is not in a human voice the strength to make itself heard in such a tumult. If the saying of the preacher were true: "The words of the wise are heard in quiet" (Sir 9:7), it would be necessary to refrain from speaking at the present time.]

The wise man keeps silent in the evil time and speaks only to the extent that he perceives his words to be of benefit, imitating God Himself, who offers us His divine mysteries only to the extent that we are able to bear hearing them, understanding them or benefiting from them. His mysteries remain hidden until we acquire the spiritual ear able to listen and to grasp the mysteries in a constructive way. From the words of St. Clement of Alexandria: [The Lord says: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear" (Mt 11:15), declaring that hearing and understanding are not for everyone. In this David writes: "He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the skies. At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed, hail stones and coals of fire" (Ps 18:11-12), showing that the sacred words are hidden.]

entries.section: 3. Injustice in the courts of justice:

paragraphs.text: The silence of the prudent in the evil time is in itself a witness of truth against injustice and tyranny... But the matter does not end there; rather the Lord demands a return to Him, through the return of these unjust judges or elders from injustice in the court of justice (in the gate), saying: "Seek good, and not evil, that ye may live: and so the LORD, the God of hosts, shall be with you, as ye have spoken" [14]. It is as though He says to them: if you boast that God, the Lord of hosts, is with you and in your midst, then the sign of this is practical conduct: seeking good and rejecting evil; by this you live by the Lord who dwells in your midst.

Israel wrongly supposed that God's choice of them as a people exempted them from punishment however much they sinned, and that God dwells in their midst whatever their condition. So God corrects their notions, declaring that His choice of them from among all the families of the earth increases their responsibility and brings them all the more under punishment if they sin (Amos 3:2). And here He affirms that His dwelling in their midst will come only by their seeking the greatest good and rejecting evil in practice in their life and their judgments. Finally, He speaks of His choice of them as making them like grain in a sieve in God's hands: He punishes them severely and deals strictly with them without destroying them (Amos 9:7-10).

entries.section: 3. Injustice in the courts of justice:

paragraphs.text: At the beginning of the sermon He said to them, "Seek the LORD" (Amos 3:6), and here He declares their obligation to seek Him through their practical conduct: "Hate the evil, and love the good, and establish judgment in the gate: it may be that the LORD God of hosts will be gracious unto the remnant of Joseph" [15]. Israel will be subjected to bitter chastisements; some of them will die, some will be killed by the sword, and some will be taken captive... But God does not forget the remnant faithful to Him. If it stands firm in the truth, loves the good and hates the evil, He will be gracious to it and declare His dwelling in its midst.

16 Therefore the LORD, the God of hosts, the Lord, saith thus; "Wailing shall be in all streets; and they shall say in all the highways, Alas! alas! and they shall call the husbandman to mourning, and such as are skilful of lamentation to wailing. 17 And in all vineyards shall be wailing: for I will pass through thee, saith the LORD."

He concludes the lamentation with God's passing through their midst, not as the secret of their life but to punish and chastise them, so that all Israel turns into a place of mourning and wailing, since all have come into a state of death. God's presence became a cause of sorrow, not of joy!
Here he presents a realistic picture of the ancient Eastern mourning, where they hired people who specialized in mournful songs during the funeral rites.
This group is in fact part of the third sermon, in which God proclaims woe to the people because of three things:

entries.section: First: desiring the day of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 18 Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD! to what end is it for you? the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light. 19 As if a man did flee from a lion, and a bear met him; or went into the house, and leaned his hand on the wall, and a serpent bit him. 20 Shall not the day of the LORD be darkness, and not light? even very dark, and no brightness in it? [18-20].

God is light, and His day is light in itself, but for the spiritually blind, who cannot behold the light, the light becomes darkness. As St. Basil says: [The day of the Lord is darkness for those who deserve darkness.]

The day of the Lord in the mind of the Jews meant God's declaring His power and His victory in His people against their enemies. Therefore it was a day of joy and triumph, a day of boasting over the Gentiles. But since the people were entangled in their many sins and unrepentant transgressions, it was turned into a day of judgment and bitterness.

No one can flee from judgment, for the one who flees is like one who flees from a lion and meets a fierce bear, or one who wants to take refuge in his house and puts his hand on a wall to lean on it, and a serpent bites him.

This is a clear line in most of the writings of the prophets, for Israel did evil and went to the holy places for public worship, offering burnt offerings and gifts and rejoicing in the feasts... God is not deceived by outward appearances, for He asks first for the heart (Mk 12:33).

In bitterness He rebukes them: "21 I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies (your gatherings). 22 Though ye offer me burnt offerings and your meat offerings, I will not accept them: neither will I regard the peace offerings of your fat beasts. 23 Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols. 24 But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." [21-24]. He rejects outward worship that is not joined to inner love, and He ascribed all the worship to them, not to Himself, saying: "your feast days, your burnt offerings," whereas when God is pleased with them, He reckons them as His feasts, His sabbaths and His burnt offerings, and rejoices to ascribe them to Himself.

God cannot bear their praises and hymns, and reckons them as noise: "the noise of thy songs." As the Apostle Paul says: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal" (1 Cor 13:1).

In order that their worship might be acceptable He says: "Let judgment (justice) run down as waters, and righteousness (almsgiving) as a mighty stream"... that is, let your life be mingled with justice and the love of giving, instead of injustice and cruelty.

"25 Have ye offered unto me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, O house of Israel? 26 But ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god, which ye made to yourselves. 27 Therefore will I cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus, saith the LORD, whose name is The God of hosts." [25-27].

The prophets looked back to the period of the wilderness as the best period Israel lived in its relationship with God (Hos 2:14-16; Jer 2:1-3), as an ideal period in which God provided for Israel in a unique and surpassing way. In this period the Lord did not stress the laws of sacrifices but the moral commandments, and perhaps their wandering in the wilderness made the offering of sacrifices difficult, so we hear that they did not keep the Passover after the second year until their crossing into Canaan.
Note here that the prophet Amos did not say: "You did not offer sacrifices and offerings," for he did not deny them altogether, but they were not a goal during their wandering in the wilderness.

They mixed the worship of God with idolatry, carrying the tabernacle of "Molech" or "Milcom," the god of the Ammonites, as a god for themselves, heating his arms until they glowed red and then placing children on them amid the beating of drums. They also worshipped gods that are a group of stars and planets. Therefore, as they took themselves captive to idolatrous worship, God humbles them by captivity under the power of idolaters, beyond Damascus (Aram), that is, to the Assyrian captivity, which is far beyond Damascus. They carried idolatry in their heart, so God left them to be carried by the idolaters!

1 Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came! 2 Pass ye unto Calneh, and see; and from thence go ye to Hamath the great: then go down to Gath of the Philistines: be they better than these kingdoms? or their border greater than your border? 3 Ye that put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near; 4 That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall; 5 That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David; 6 That drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph. 7 Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed.
"Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came!" [1].

He pronounces the woe perhaps upon the great men, the nobles, and all who held religious and civil leadership in Judah and Israel, for they had become secure and settled down in Zion and Samaria, in a life of luxury and pampering, especially since they were counted as chief of the nations, that is, they were more exalted and honored than all the nations, or they were the firstfruits of the nations.

Zion was known for its towers and bulwarks, as the Psalmist says: "Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof. Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following" (Ps 48:12-13); it contained within it the thrones of the house of David (Ps 122:5). As for the mountain of Samaria, it had become the center of religious life for the northern kingdom. The great men in both regions lounged in security, since civil power and religious leadership were in their hands; the nations feared them and the house of Israel came to them.

This is the state of the soul that finds for itself a refuge other than God: it feels secure because of its temporal success or its religious reputation; everyone looks at it with honor and admiration, and in foolishness it settles down and rests secure, instead of continual striving and growth in the Lord.

To rouse the people of Zion and the mountain of Samaria to repentance, the Lord gave them examples of great cities that had borne a reputation for a long time and had perished. He mentioned Calneh, which Nimrod built in the land of Shinar (Gen 10:10) and which was utterly ruined; Hamath in Syria, whose gods Sennacherib boasted that he had destroyed (2 Kgs 18:34); and Gath in Philistia, which Hazael had ruined a short time before (2 Kgs 12:17)... Are Zion and the mountain of Samaria better than these cities, or is their border greater than their border?

Truly, it is fitting that we take warning from what happens to others. If sin has shattered giants, and negligence has ruined kingdoms, it is fitting for us not to accept sin and not to walk in laxity, lest we become an example and a warning like the others!

Israel did not take warning from what befell the kingdoms around it, and paid no heed to God's threats to it, absorbed in its injustice even in the courts of justice, supposing that chastisement would not come upon it soon. "Ye that put far away the evil day (the chastisement), and cause the seat of violence to come near" [3].

This life, marked by settling into evil and injustice and by indifference to God's warnings, was supported by their luxurious and pampered life, for their hearts were drawn into pleasures and lusts. God rebukes them, saying:
"That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall (the manger)" [4].

Their life was marked by sleep and slackness; they spent their time lying on beds inlaid with ivory and stretched out on their couches, eating many of the lambs and the fatted calves... People who know nothing of spiritual striving and seriousness: instead of the sackcloth that they ought to have girded themselves with because of their sins, they stretched themselves on beds all the days of their life, and instead of fasting and humility they eat greedily. As the Apostle Paul says of some wicked teachers: "For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly" (Rom 16:18). And in another place he says: "Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things. For our conversation is in heaven" (Phil 3:19-20).

Thus they live for their bellies and walk as men of the dust seeking temporal pleasures, and instead of enjoying the divine heavenly praises they love a life of excessive revelry, offering corrupting songs bound up with licentious music which is the work of their own hands, whereas David offered his psalms in order to draw his heart to heaven: "That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David" [5]. Perhaps in the time of their revelry they sang some religious songs, not for repentance but in mockery, as the people of Babylon asked the people of Israel to sing the songs of Zion in the land of captivity, and they answered: "How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?" [4]. But these sang the songs of the Lord amid their revelry and drunkenness, in an atmosphere foreign to the Lord!

Pampering dominated their whole life: in their sleep, their eating, their revelry, and also in their drunkenness and their perfuming themselves with costly ointments: "That drink wine in bowls - basins, which are large bowls used for sacrificial purposes (Ex 38:3; Zech 14:20) - and anoint themselves with the chief ointments" [6].

St. Clement of Alexandria comments on these prophetic expressions, saying: [When the Holy Spirit spoke through Amos, He declared the wretchedness of the rich because of their luxurious life.] Tertullian says likewise: [Truly, (the rich) have found their consolation, their glory, their honor and the height of their position in their riches. And in Psalm 48 He turns us away from concern for these things, saying: "Be not thou afraid when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased; for when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him" (Ps 49:16-17), and in (Psalm 62) He says: "Do not desire riches, and if riches increase, set not your heart upon them" (Ps 62:10). Finally, this woe was pronounced by the prophet against the rich man who is attached to delights.] And St. John Chrysostom says: [Behold how God blames luxury also, for He does not condemn them here for greed they had committed but merely for extravagance. Here you are eating to the point of gluttony while Christ does not have what is necessary. You eat various cakes while Christ does not have dry bread. You drink Thasian wine and do not give Christ a cup of cold water, though He is thirsty. You lie on a soft embroidered bed while He perishes from cold!]

The Lord completes His description of this slack, pampered company by saying: "But they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph" [6]. This is the sin with which He closes His description of this company in order to pass judgment on it: "Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed" [7]. What is this sin with which He concludes, so that He reckons them worthy to be the first of the captives and the feasts they used to spread and stretch themselves upon to be taken away from them?

"Joseph" most often refers to Israel as a whole, as though the heart of these slack great men had withdrawn into luxury and revelry, far from the affliction that Israel was passing through, like the person who in his luxury forgets the sufferings and sorrows of the Church.

Perhaps "the affliction of Joseph" reminds us of the chief butler who returned to his work and stood before Pharaoh, and forgot Joseph in prison (Gen 40:21, 23). So when a person lives in comfort and ease, he forgets his suffering and deprived brethren... It is a hideous picture that reveals man's selfishness and his cutting himself off from his membership in the holy congregation.

Many of the Fathers link this expression "they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph" with what is written in the book of Micah (Mic 1:11): "She who dwells in Zaanan does not go forth to mourn over the place next to her" (Septuagint), saying that what befell Israel (Joseph) and the neighbors of Zaanan came by God's permission to chastise them, and yet, since we do not share their sorrow, this is counted as sin against us. As St. John Chrysostom says: [Even if they are being chastised justly, it is not fitting for you to rejoice at their harm... for God wants you to show compassion even on these. For if we, who are evil, when we punish a servant and see his fellow servant laughing, are all the more enraged and pour out our anger on the fellow servant (for his laughter), how much more will God punish those who are arrogant toward the one who is chastising them?] He also says: [Even if they are justly punished, God wants us to console them and not to rejoice or revile them. He says: "If I punish, I take no pleasure in it; I take no pleasure in the punishment of the sinner, since I do not desire his death" (Ezek 18:32). So it is fitting for you to imitate your Lord, and to grieve that the sinner has fallen under a just punishment, for whoever acquires such a good sorrow gathers great profit.]

8 The Lord GOD hath sworn by himself, saith the LORD the God of hosts, "I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces: therefore will I deliver up the city with all that is therein." 9 And it shall come to pass, if there remain ten men in one house, that they shall die. 10 And a man's uncle shall take him up, and he that burneth him, to bring out the bones out of the house, and shall say unto him that is by the sides of the house, "Is there yet any with thee?" and he shall say, "No." Then shall he say, "Hold thy tongue: for we may not make mention of the name of the LORD." 11 For, behold, the LORD commandeth, and he will smite the great house with breaches, and the little house with clefts.

God pronounces woe upon Israel because it fell into pride, saying: "I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces: therefore will I deliver up the city with all that is therein" [8]. The city that He loves and upon which His name was called, He delivers up with its palaces and all that fills it, because of its vain greatness and boasting. He abhors it and delivers it to chastisement with an oath, so that all may be certain that the judgment will not be revoked.

St. John Climacus says of pride: [Pride is a denial of God, an invention of the demons, a contempt for men, a mother of condemnation, a daughter of praises, a sign of barrenness, a flight from God's help, a forerunner of madness of mind, a promoter of falls, a cause of epilepsy, a fountain of anger, a gate of hypocrisy, a helper of demons, a guardian of sins, a patroness of hardness of heart, an ignorance of compassion, a bitter accountant and an unjust judge, an adversary of God and the root of blasphemy,] and he also says: [Wherever a fall has come, there pride has gone before and dwelt, for the presence of the one announces the coming of the other.]

Since they fell into deadly pride, He pursued them with successive chastisements, until if only ten men remained in one house they would die. He presented a bitter picture of their state: the uncle carries the body of his brother's daughter, though one would expect a man to carry the body of his father and his uncle, and offers a burning for the dead as an honor to him (Jer 34:5; 2 Chr 16:14; 21:19), and when he asks who is in the house he finds that all have died, so that hearts rage against the Lord (Prov 19:3) and do not mention His name. Thus the ruin reaches the houses of Israel until there is no one to mention the name of the Lord. And the strange thing is that the Lord smites the great house with destruction and the little house so that it becomes clefts; He shatters the great before the small, and more violently, because of his increasing pride!

12 Shall horses run upon the rock? will one plow there with oxen? for ye have turned judgment into gall, and the fruit of righteousness into hemlock: 13 Ye which rejoice in a thing of nought, which say, "Have we not taken to us horns by our own strength?" 14 "But, behold, I will raise up against you a nation, O house of Israel, saith the LORD the God of hosts; and they shall afflict you from the entering in of Hemath unto the river of the wilderness."

The third reason for their falling under the woes is: "Ye which rejoice in a thing of nought, which say, Have we not taken to us horns by our own strength?" [13]. They rejoice amid their pampering and luxury as though nothing would befall them, or as though what is said to them by way of warnings were vain words, relying on themselves and their strength... And this is the secret of their failure, for they close against themselves every way of escape, as He says: "Shall horses run upon the rock? will one plow there with oxen? for ye have turned judgment into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood" [12]. It is as though He says to them: I sent the prophets to you carrying warnings for your repentance and your return to me, and they found your hearts rock, upon which horses cannot run, nor oxen plow. You have turned judgment into poison and bitterness! You have made truth and righteousness lose their taste and benefit! Therefore He concludes His sermon by sending a nation to afflict them from every side: from the north "the entering in of Hemath," and from the south "the river of the wilderness" (the Arabah), which is a valley south of the Dead Sea as far as the Gulf of Aqaba...

1 Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me; and, behold, he formed grasshoppers in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and, lo, it was the latter growth after the king's mowings. 2 And it came to pass, that when they had made an end of eating the grass of the land, then I said, "O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small." 3 The LORD repented for this: "It shall not be," saith the LORD.

God had already threatened Israel through the prophet Amos that He would send locusts to eat their gardens, their vineyards, their fig trees and their olive trees (Amos 4:9), and now He showed him His plan, which was mingled with justice and mercy together; while He chastises, He was showing tenderness, and while He plans, He awaits a word of intercession from the prophet so that He may stop the chastisement [3].

He sent locusts that He Himself had prepared [1], for He entrusts no one with the chastisement of His children; even if He uses locusts or enemies, the hand of God remains the One who directs, and His eyes are upon them, like the potter who attends to the vessels he has placed in the furnace for a time. He prepared the locusts, but in their stage as larvae (at the beginning of the shooting up) [1], and they appeared after the king's mowings (that is, after the first harvest which was given as tribute to the king). He did not allow the locusts to eat the crop before the first harvest so that they might live on what they had already reaped as tribute to the king and not perish of hunger. It is as though, while He chastises, He does not permit destruction; so He let them reap the first harvest, and then destroyed the harvest with the locusts. As the Psalmist says: "O forsake me not utterly" (Ps 119:8), or "do not forsake me for long"; for in chastisement God seems to have forsaken us, but only until we return to Him, and then He returns to us.

The prophet interceded for Israel in humility, saying: "O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small" [2]. This is the Jacob of whom God said, "I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces" (Amos 6:8). As soon as the prophet interceded for him, saying that he is small and cannot bear the chastisement, the Lord repented and stopped, not in the sense of changing His mind concerning him but in the sense of changing the situation itself.

Even in the bitterest moments of our chastisement, God longs to hear the voice of Amos in us interceding before Him in a spirit of humility, declaring that we are small and in need of Him, so that He lifts His chastisement and embraces us.
Some scholars see that the locust campaign was one of the attacks against Israel, whether stirred up by Aram or Assyria or others.

entries.section: 2. The vision of the destroying fire:

paragraphs.text: 4 Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me: and, behold, the Lord GOD called to contend by fire, and it devoured the great deep, and did eat up a part. 5 Then said I, "O Lord GOD, cease, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small." 6 The LORD repented for this: "This also shall not be," saith the Lord GOD.

The first time God chastised with extreme tenderness, and since Israel did not turn back from its sin to God, He returned to chastise more severely; this time He does not chastise them in a hidden way but openly: "The Lord GOD called to contend by fire" [4]. As was said by the prophet Isaiah: "For, behold, the LORD will come with fire, and with his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his anger with fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire and by his sword will the LORD plead with all flesh: and the slain of the LORD shall be many" (Isa 66:15-16), as he also said: "The LORD standeth up to plead, and standeth to judge the people" (Isa 3:13), and also: "Wherefore I will yet plead with you, saith the LORD, and with your children's children will I plead" (Jer 2:9), "For the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land" (Hos 4:1).

God calls to an open trial not in order to take vengeance by our human understanding, but in order to turn the wicked from his wickedness by the fire of chastisement, burning up his sins, so that he returns to Him and enjoys His divine love.

In the first chastisement He was content with part of the harvest, but this time, as He chastises more firmly, He deprives them of water and food: the fire devours the great deep and the field, so that a person feels the need for One who will water him and satisfy him... and finds in God his drink and his food.
This time also God awaits the intercession of His prophet in order to forgive His people.

7 Thus he shewed me: and, behold, the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand. 8 And the LORD said unto me, "Amos, what seest thou?" And I said, "A plumbline." Then said the Lord, "Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more: 9 And the high places of Isaac shall be desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste; and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword."

The Lord stood before the wall with the plumbline (a measure by which the straightness of a wall is known); God measured the kingdom of Israel with His divine plumbline and said: "I will not again pass by them any more" [8].

It was fitting for the Jewish Church to be a wall of faith in the Messiah, but she rejected this work and denied her Savior... This is what God's plumbline revealed, and so she deserved to be torn down. So too souls that receive a spiritual leadership task, if they are not faithful and do not walk as a wall for others supporting them in their spiritual striving, deserve to be torn down.

The Lord says through Isaiah: "Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet" (Isa 28:17), and the prophet David measured the Moabites with a line, to put to death and with one full line to keep alive (1 Sam 8:2), and when Manasseh king of Judah did evil, the Lord said: "And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down" (2 Kgs 21:13).

Perhaps His use of the plumbline means that He offers His divine chastisements by measure, with great precision, according to what we can bear and according to our need for building up, although it is preceded by the tearing down of what is crooked in us.

The prophet continues his speech: "And the high places of Isaac shall be desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste; and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword" [9]. What does he mean by this destruction? If they take refuge in the high places and reckon that the sanctuaries fortify them and that their present king is strong, then their high places become a wasteland, their sanctuaries a ruin, and their king Jeroboam with all his house are given over to slaughter.

In the age of the patriarchs the high places were considered the best place for setting up altars and offering sacrifices to the Lord, perhaps because they are elevated... as though man in his relation with God rises above earthly and temporal things. But the Jews' mixing with the Gentiles led them to set up idolatrous altars on the high places, so the prophets rose up attacking the high places as a symbol of idolatry, especially since the Lord now had His temple in Jerusalem, and it was not permitted to offer sacrifices outside it.
Perhaps He chose "the high places of Isaac" because "Isaac" means (laughter), as though they would become a laughingstock and a mockery among the nations because of the destruction that befalls them.
As for the sword that rises against the house of Jeroboam the Second, it is the sword of Assyria.

10 Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, "Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words. 11 For thus Amos saith, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be led away captive out of their own land."

Instead of Israel, with its king, its leaders, its priests and its people, offering repentance, as the people of Nineveh did when they heard the prophet Jonah rebuking them, the priest of Bethel informs against the prophet Amos to King Jeroboam the Second, saying: "Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words. For thus Amos saith, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be led away captive out of their own land" [10-11].

Instead of Amaziah doing his work as a priest proclaiming the truth, he turns the truth into wormwood; he made of Amos's prophecies a conspiracy against the king in the midst of the people, and counted the prophet's words not a message of repentance and the building up of the community but an agitation of the people against the king and his men! The priest's heart had turned away from service to temporal positions, earthly glory and love of the world, so it is no wonder that he distorts the prophet's message and disfigures the divine work, as though it were a work against the king and the people... as though it were national treason!

He says to the king, "the land is not able to bear all his words," suggesting to the king that the whole people are against Amos and that his preaching is intolerable to everyone. These are the words of the enemy of good in every age, as he suggests to people that God's words are unacceptable and preaching the Gospel is intolerable and unrealistic, in order to turn them aside from God's work and take them outside the circle of the Cross.

He says "the land is not able to bear all his words"... Truly, the priest Amaziah was earth and not heaven, and could not bear the prophet's words. The carnal man is a man of dust who walks with an earthly mind, so he does not accept what belongs to God and cannot endure the heavenly life; therefore "the land is not able to bear all his words."

When the Lord Christ spoke of His holy Body and Blood, given as the secret of eternal life, many of His disciples said: "This is an hard saying; who can hear it?... From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him" (Jn 6:60, 66).

"12 Also Amaziah said unto Amos, 'O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: 13 But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court.'" [12-13].

Amaziah supposed of Amos that he was a prophet in order to eat bread, but Amos was not so; he prophesies not as a job to live from, but because he is an instrument in the hand of God his Creator. It is no wonder that the priest drives out the prophet, for the latter, despite his simplicity, by his faithfulness and courage uncovers the secret of the former and exposes his life.

St. Jerome says: [Amos was driven out of Samaria. Why? Surely because here, as in other cases, he is a spiritual surgeon who cuts off the members infected with sin, and urges the people to repentance. The Apostle Paul says: "Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?" (Gal 4:16)].

Amos was not an official prophet from the school of the prophets, who acquired prophecy by learning or inheritance... but he was faithful in the eyes of God, better than the holder of official authority, the priest of Bethel. Therefore St. Jerome says in one of his letters: [Not all bishops are truly bishops. You look at Peter; observe Judas also. You look at Stephen; see Nicodemus, who was condemned in the Apocalypse by the very lips of the Lord (Amos 2:6), who raised up the heresy of the Nicolaitans through his imaginations. Therefore "let a man examine himself" (1 Cor 11:28) and come; it is not ecclesiastical rank that makes him a Christian!]

14 Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: 15 And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel. 16 Now therefore hear thou the word of the LORD: Thou sayest, Prophesy not against Israel, and drop not thy word against the house of Isaac. 17 Therefore thus saith the LORD; Thy wife shall be an harlot in the city, and thy sons and thy daughters shall fall by the sword, and thy land shall be divided by line; and thou shalt die in a polluted land: and Israel shall surely go into captivity forth of his land."

In humility filled with courage Amos said to Amaziah: "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: and the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel" [14-15].

In humility he did not deny his former lowly work as a shepherd of sheep and a gatherer of sycamore fruit, and in courage he declared that it was the Lord who called him from behind the sheep to prophesy to God's people Israel... He is not a prophet in the minds of some, because he was not trained in the school of the prophets and did not inherit prophecy, so he is not a son of a prophet, but he is a prophet by a personal call from God, and so he is bound to do the work given by the One who called him.

St. John Chrysostom says: [He did not say this to boast of himself (that God called him to prophecy), but to silence the mouths of those who supposed that he was not a prophet, showing them that he is not a deceiver and does not speak anything of his own accord.]

St. Gregory of Nazianzus speaks of the Holy Spirit who worked in Amos to raise him up as a prophet, saying: [This Spirit, being all-wise and all-loving, when He takes possession of a shepherd makes him a psalmist who drives away evil spirits with his psalm (1 Sam 16:23), and when He acquires a shepherd of sheep and gatherer of sycamore fruit makes him a prophet. Remember David and Amos!]

Finally, in boldness the prophet Amos did not keep silent but declared to him that his wife would be a harlot, his sons and daughters would fall by the sword, his land would be divided by line, and he himself would die in a polluted land and Israel would be led away captive from its land. Perhaps this was fulfilled literally at the captivity of Israel by Assyria, when one of the attacking soldiers committed evil with Amaziah's wife, and he lost his sons and daughters, while he was carried to an idolatrous land to die there.

How bitter it is when the priest of the Lord or his son becomes corrupt, so that the Lord abandons him to corrupt his body like Amaziah's wife who committed adultery, and he loses his gifts and abilities, which are scattered like Amaziah's sons and daughters slain by the sword, and instead of inheriting he loses what he has, so that strangers divide his land and he falls into disgrace, and because of him also the Church is led captive, as many fall and stumble!

entries.section: 1. A basket for the bitter gathering:

paragraphs.text: 1 Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me: and behold a basket of summer fruit. 2 And he said, "Amos, what seest thou?" And I said, "A basket of summer fruit." Then said the LORD unto me, "The end is come upon my people of Israel; I will not again pass by them any more. 3 And the songs of the temple shall be howlings in that day, saith the Lord GOD: there shall be many dead bodies in every place; they shall cast them forth with silence."

God showed him a basket for gathering; in Hebrew the word means "fruit at the end of summer or in the autumn." The time had come to eat the fruit, but it is not joyful fruit; it is the ripened fruit of sin, which cannot be waited upon. The time of dark winter had drawn near, and it was necessary to eat the fruit that does not remain for the winter!

entries.section: 1. A basket for the bitter gathering:

paragraphs.text: God gave them many opportunities to repent of their sins and return to Him, at one time by declarations, at another by gifts and kindnesses, and at a third by threats... He used to chastise so that He might return and forgive, but now they have prepared themselves for destruction... "The end is come upon my people of Israel" [2]. He does not forget that they are His people, but their end has come because of their persistence in their evil, as He says: "I will not again pass by them any more" [2]. The songs of the palace (the temple) and their joys turn into mourning and weeping, and instead of joy corpses without number are gathered in silence, when they see the temple become a ruin and the distress too great to be borne, or because they find no strength to weep for the multitude of the dead; and perhaps the silence is also a sign of fear of the enemy, lest he hear their voices and come and kill the remnant that is left!

Though God is very longsuffering, as the Apostle says: "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; who will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:4-6).

God in His love watches in us for a sign toward Him so that He may return to us; He longs to dwell in us and to enter with us into His glories. But if we hold fast to refusal and walk in evil, our sins ripen to be gathered as in the bitter basket of gathering, which the Lord cannot bear, and our end comes though we are His children, and our sonship to Him becomes a secret of torment for the soul and a testimony of judgment, and instead of songs of joy it becomes a wailing of the soul, which finds the temple emptied and everything within it of gifts and endowments finished! Let us then return to Him and He will return to us, that we may have within us His joyful paradise instead of this sorrowful basket!

4 Hear this, O ye that swallow up the needy, even to make the poor of the land to fail, 5 Saying, "When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit? 6 That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; yea, and sell the refuse of the wheat?" 7 The LORD hath sworn by the excellency of Jacob, "Surely I will never forget any of their works. 8 Shall not the land tremble for this, and every one mourn that dwelleth therein? and it shall rise up wholly as a flood; and it shall be cast out and drowned, as by the flood of Egypt. 9 And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord GOD, that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day: 10 And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring up sackcloth upon all loins, and baldness upon every head; and I will make it as the mourning of an only son, and the end thereof as a bitter day."
The prophet presents to us a picture of the state of injustice and corruption in which Israel lived at that time. Among its features:

First: he says, "Hear this, O ye that swallow up the needy, even to make the poor of the land to fail" [4]. They want to crush the poor; they long to swallow them in their bellies or trample them under their feet, to make the poor of the land to fail. In their love of themselves they permit themselves injustice, even the utter destruction of the poor and needy by every means, for the sake of their wealth, their belly and their revelry!

When the ego swells, a person thinks himself the center of the world; everyone works for his account and everyone perishes for the sake of his happiness. But of the Lord of glory Jesus it was said: "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich" (2 Cor 8:9). When we carry Him in us we are enriched by Him, and the sign of our riches is that we accept to become poor with Him so that our brethren may be enriched by Christ who dwells in us. We long to be enslaved so that they may be freed in Him, to die so that they may enjoy life with Him, and to leave everything so that they may possess it as the secret of their wealth. Thus our teacher the Apostle Paul walked in the spirit of his Master when he said: "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more" (1 Cor 9:20), "For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake" (2 Cor 4:5).

Second: "Saying, When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat" [5]. They fulfill the Law to the letter and stop work on the new moon and every sabbath, as though they were religious and lovers of God, but these days pass over them very heavily, for they long for them to pass so that they may return to their trade and material gain. In the eyes of people, and perhaps in their own eyes, they are righteous, hallowing the feast days and sabbaths, but their heart in reality is not sanctified, for it is occupied with profit and matter, even if work has stopped outwardly! As it was said: "For with their mouth they shew much love, but their heart goeth after their covetousness" (Ezek 33:31).

It is a painful picture of the soul that has become earth, which finds the day of the Lord burdensome, and feels in worship that it is long and without profit, while it spends most of its time rejoicing in material gains!
Third: "Making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit" [5]. It is said in Proverbs, "A false balance is abomination to the LORD" (Prov 11:1).

Some explain their making the ephah small and the shekel great as meaning that they sell to people by the ephah and cheat them by making it smaller than it ought to be, and when they buy wholesale they buy by the shekel, and make it larger to cheat the farmers who sell to them. It is as though they steal in their dealings, in buying as in selling, for their own account.

Fourth: "That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; yea, and sell the refuse of the wheat" [6]. In our study of the second chapter the Lord says: "They sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes" (Amos 2:6), and we saw that in reality they sell the Lord, the only Righteous One, for the sake of material things, and they despise Him in the person of the poor and needy for a pair of shoes. He had earlier commanded Moses to take them off (Ex 3), and the disciples not to acquire them (Mt 10:10).

They buy the weak for silver; when the poor fell into extreme misery they would go to the rich of their own people and sell themselves and their children to them as slaves for the price of food, so that they might be able to live, a matter that later stirred up Nehemiah (Neh 5).

As for their selling the refuse of the wheat, in it is a violation of the Law and a removal of love, for it ought to have been left for the poor who cannot afford to buy wheat to enjoy, so that they might take the refuse. On this principle it is written in the book of Deuteronomy: "When thou cuttest down thine harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go again to fetch it: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands..." (Deut 24:19).

When Israel, the people of God, reached this bitter state, it fell under severe trial, as the prophet says: "The LORD hath sworn by the excellency of Jacob, Surely I will never forget any of their works. Shall not the land tremble for this, and every one mourn that dwelleth therein? and it shall rise up wholly as a flood; and it shall be cast out and drowned, as by the flood of Egypt. And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord GOD, that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day: and I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring up sackcloth upon all loins, and baldness upon every head; and I will make it as the mourning of an only son, and the end thereof as a bitter day" [7-10].

With all the injustice and iniquity that Israel committed, so that the Lord swore He would never forget any of these evil works of theirs, that is, He would forgive no more, He still holds a special affection for them, for He says: "The LORD hath sworn by the excellency of Jacob"... We are His children; He boasts of us and longs for our salvation despite what we have done and the wrong we have done to Him.

Before the injustice of this people the whole land trembled and its inhabitants mourned, and it rose up as a flood and began to shake as in an earthquake, like the River Nile which overflows with water at the time of the flood and then its water falls again! The sun cannot look upon this evil, so it goes down at noon and the earth turns to darkness instead of light, and the feasts are turned into mourning and the songs into lamentations, and people put on sackcloth instead of adornment, and become like one who has lost his only son, in bitter anguish.

It is a natural bitter fruit tasted by the one whose cup is filled with evil, for his land, that is, his body that offers him pleasures, trembles before God and loses its vitality, and all its inhabitants mourn, that is, his senses and feelings lose all joy, to enter a state of despair and discontent; a person's life shakes as in an earthquake, and he becomes like the Nile of Egypt, constantly rising and falling without stability. The Sun of Righteousness sets for him, so he loses all the enlightenment he had once enjoyed, and his inner land turns into the gloom of ignorance. He does not know spiritual joy, but his inner feasts turn into a funeral, and instead of praise he utters lamentations, and instead of inner spiritual adornment he is in disgrace like one who wears sackcloth. His life turns like that of one at a funeral, so he shaves the hair of his head to become bald, and weeps like one who has lost his only son, who is his own one soul!

And the wonder is that the Lord carried this bitter fruit for us when He bowed His back to the Cross, "and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isa 53:6). So this prophecy was fulfilled literally. The earth trembled, as the Evangelist says: "And the earth did quake, and the rocks rent; and the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose" (Mt 27:51-52).

The earth quaked, and Hades also quaked. And the sun went down at noon, as the same Evangelist says: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour" (Mt 27:45). And the feasts of the Jews were afterwards turned into mourning and their songs into lamentations, since they lost the temple and were scattered through all the lands and lost their position as the people of God, so they became like those in the mourning for an only son.
Many of the Fathers saw in these words a striking prophecy of what happened during the Passion of the Lord Christ, among them Father Lactantius, Tertullian the teacher, and St. Irenaeus.

St. Irenaeus says: [He announced clearly that the eclipse of the sun at the time of His crucifixion would take place at the sixth hour and after (Amos 8:9); after this their feasts according to the Law and their songs would be turned into sorrow and wailing when they are delivered to the Gentiles.] In the same sense Tertullian the teacher says: [You were taken captive and scattered after the Passion of Christ, as the Holy Spirit had foretold.] As Isaiah also says: "I clothe the heavens with blackness" (Isa 50:3). This is the day of which Amos writes: "And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord GOD, that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day." For at noon the veil of the temple was rent, as the cherubim fled (Ezek 11:22-23), when "the daughter of Zion is left as a cottage in a vineyard, as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers" (Isa 1:8)].

St. John Chrysostom gives a spiritual understanding, in our daily life, of the eclipse of the sun and the coming of darkness upon the earth, saying: [It seems to me that not only the earth, but even the nature of the air and the circle of the sun's rays look on with sorrow, so that its rays became all the more clouded (dark), not because its elements have changed, but because our eyes are troubled with clouds of sorrow and have become unable to see the light of the rays clearly... This is what the prophet wept over long ago when he said: "I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day." He says this not because the planet of the day was eclipsed or the day disappeared, but because those who are in sorrow cannot perceive the light of noon because of the darkness of their blindness.] We need God to remove from us the darkness of sin, so that our eyes may be enlightened by His Holy Spirit to behold Jesus Christ the Sun of Righteousness and to enjoy His splendor in us!

As for the turning of the feasts into sorrow and the songs into mourning, this is the natural work of sin, while repentance gives us the opposite in Christ Jesus, for to Him we return, and in Him we find our feast truly joyful and delightful. As St. Gregory the Wonderworker says: [It is our duty to keep this feast, seeing that it fills the whole world with joy and gladness. Let us keep it with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs... Our Lord has assured us that He turns our sorrows into joy through the fruit of repentance.]

entries.section: 3. A famine for the words of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 11 "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD: 12 And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east, they shall run to and fro to seek the word of the LORD, and shall not find it. 13 In that day shall the fair virgins and young men faint for thirst. 14 They that swear by the sin of Samaria, and say, Thy god, O Dan, liveth; and, The manner of Beersheba liveth; even they shall fall, and never rise up again."

The fruit of sin is shattering from every side: a bodily shattering, where the land trembles and every one mourns that dwelleth therein [8]; a psychological shattering, where the soul loses its light and turns into a state of gloom and is in unceasing mourning; and finally a spiritual shattering, where a person loses his spiritual food, as He says: "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD... In that day shall the fair virgins and young men faint for thirst" [11-13].

entries.section: 3. A famine for the words of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: This is what God threatens the wicked with: that they enter into a hunger and thirst not for bread and water but for the life-giving words of the Lord. They wander from sea to sea, that is, from a teacher marked by the temporal character, for the sea refers to the world with its troubled waves; they seek satisfaction for their souls and peace from teachers who are deprived of spiritual satisfaction and true peace; they search in all parts of the world from the north to the south... but in vain, until all their gifts, abilities and possibilities fade away from spiritual thirst, and the fair virgins and strong young men die of thirst! They realize the sin of Samaria, and seek the strange gods in the north, "Dan," and in the south, "the way of Beersheba," "even they shall fall, and never rise up again" [14].

It is a terrible famine in which the soul seeks spiritual satisfaction and does not find it, not because God has deprived it, but because, through its multiplied sins and its unwillingness to repent, it loses its perception of the word of God as the bread of life.

Would that we might always enjoy the word of the Lord, of which the Master Himself says: "The words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life" (Jn 6:63). And St. John Chrysostom says: [(The word of God) is the food of the soul, its adornment, and its pledge; in not hearing it there is famine and deprivation.]
